# One missing value: accident, clue, or problem? {#sec-eda-missing-data}













In @sec-eda-first-look, `skim()` told us that exactly one value in `cell_data` is missing: `Pdgfrb_Neg`, animal `Td79`. One cell out of 980 (49 rows times 20 columns), about 0.1% of the table. It would be perfectly reasonable to shrug. I did, the first time. Then I asked myself the question this chapter is built around:

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***Is this NA an accident, a clue, or a problem?***
:::

An accident is a value that went missing for a reason that has nothing to do with the biology (a dropped slide), and that costs you a little precision and nothing else. A clue is a missing value that tells you something about how the data were produced, and therefore about whether the rest of the numbers can be trusted. A problem is a missing value that, if you handle it carelessly, changes your answer. A single `NA` could in principle be any of the three, and the honest thing to say at the outset is that one cell cannot tell us which. What I can do is show you how to look, what the standard ways of thinking about missingness assume, and what each way of dealing with it costs. I should also warn you that this particular `NA` is a very small stage for a very large topic: several of the plots below will illustrate a method more than they will discover anything, and I will say so when that happens.

## Looking at a single missing value

When I first learned to look for missing data in R, I used `is.na()` and `colSums()`, and they work. But a table of counts is a poor way to *see* the pattern, in the same way a list of well coordinates is a poor way to see which wells of a plate failed. The packages `naniar` [@naniar] and `visdat` [@visdat] exist to draw that plate map. They treat missingness as data worth plotting in its own right, and they both return ordinary `ggplot2` objects, so everything we add on top (the book's `Plot_theme`, a colorblind-safe palette) works exactly as it does for any other figure.

Start with the most literal picture. `vis_miss()` draws the whole table as a grid, one row per animal and one column per variable, and colors each cell by whether the value is there. I like it as a first look precisely because it makes no decision for you: you see the table, with the holes. It is a heatmap of a binary variable, which is the right chart when the thing you want to locate is *where*, in two dimensions, something happens.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
vis_miss(cell_data, show_perc = FALSE, show_perc_col = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("grey85", okabe_ito[["missing"]]),
    labels = c("Present", "Missing")
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Animal (row)", fill = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 0, size = 10),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.position = "top",
        plot.margin = margin(5, 40, 5, 5))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Every cell of `cell_data`, colored by whether it is present. Rows are the 49 animals, columns are the 20 variables. Exactly one cell is missing: `Pdgfrb_Neg` for animal `Td79`.](eda-missing-data_files/figure-html/fig-missing-vismiss-1.png){#fig-missing-vismiss fig-alt='Grid of 49 rows and 20 columns. Almost every cell is the same pale color, indicating observed values. A single dark cell appears in the Pdgfrb_Neg column near the bottom of the grid.' width=864}
:::
:::






One orange cell in a sea of gray. This is the moment to be candid: for a dataset this size the figure adds nothing that `skim()` had not already told us. Where `vis_miss()` earns its keep is on a spreadsheet with hundreds of columns, where a missing block (every measurement from one batch of animals, say) lines up as a stripe and you see in half a second what no summary table would show. I am using it here because you should meet the tool on a dataset where you can verify every cell by eye.

The second view collapses the grid into a count per variable. `gg_miss_var()` is a bar chart, and bars are the right encoding for an amount, as long as they start at zero, which these do.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gg_miss_var(cell_data) +
  labs(y = "Missing values (count)") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Number of missing values per variable, sorted. Nineteen variables have none; `Pdgfrb_Neg` has one.](eda-missing-data_files/figure-html/fig-missing-missvar-1.png){#fig-missing-missvar fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of the count of missing values for each variable in cell_data. Only the Pdgfrb_Neg bar has nonzero length, with a value of one.' width=672}
:::
:::






Same lesson, a different encoding: it is a ranked list of problems, which is useful when twenty variables compete for your attention, and nearly pointless when there is a single entry on it.

The third view is the one I would keep even for this dataset, because it asks a question the first two cannot: *where in the rest of the data does the missing value sit?* `geom_miss_point()` is a scatterplot that does not throw away points with a missing coordinate. Instead it parks them on a stripe just below (or left of) the axis, in a different color, so you can ask whether the missing animal looks like its neighbors. For `Td79`, we know its `Pdgfrb_Pos` count, so we can see where it would sit in the vertical direction, even though its horizontal position is unknown. I color the missing one and also label it directly with its ID, so it stays identifiable in a grayscale printout of the PDF edition.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Where geom_miss_point() parks the missing animal, so we can label it directly
neg_range <- range(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg, na.rm = TRUE)
parked <- cell_data |>
  filter(is.na(Pdgfrb_Neg)) |>
  mutate(Pdgfrb_Neg = neg_range[1] - 0.1 * diff(neg_range))   # naniar's default stripe

ggplot(cell_data, aes(x = Pdgfrb_Neg, y = Pdgfrb_Pos)) +
  geom_miss_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = parked, aes(label = MouseID),
                           nudge_y = 500, size = 5, color = okabe_ito[["missing"]],
                           min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Missing" = okabe_ito[["missing"]],
                                "Not Missing" = okabe_ito[["observed"]])) +
  labs(x = "PDGFR-β negative cells (Pdgfrb_Neg)",
       y = "PDGFR-β positive cells (Pdgfrb_Pos)",
       color = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![`Pdgfrb_Pos` against `Pdgfrb_Neg`. The animal with a missing `Pdgfrb_Neg` (orange, labeled `Td79`) is parked just left of the observed range, at the height of its known `Pdgfrb_Pos`. That position on the horizontal axis is not data: it is a place to put the point so you can see it.](eda-missing-data_files/figure-html/fig-missing-misspoint-1.png){#fig-missing-misspoint fig-alt='Scatter plot of PDGFR-beta positive cell counts on the vertical axis against PDGFR-beta negative cell counts on the horizontal axis. Blue points are scattered across the plot. One orange point labeled Td79 sits slightly to the left of the lowest horizontal value, at a vertical position near 400.' width=672}
:::
:::






There is nothing odd about where the triangle sits vertically: a count near 400 is unremarkable for `Pdgfrb_Pos`, and the day-3 animals cluster at low counts anyway. That is mildly reassuring and, with one point, proves nothing.

One more `naniar` function deserves a mention because it is the one everyone wants to try. `gg_miss_upset()` draws an UpSet plot: it counts how often *combinations* of variables are missing together, which is the right question when many variables go missing in patterns (a failed channel takes three measurements with it). Let me run it, because the result is itself informative.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tryCatch(
  gg_miss_upset(cell_data),
  error = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e))
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
upset plots for missing data requre at least two variables to have missing data, only one variable, 'Pdgfrb_Neg' has missing values.
```


:::
:::






It refuses, and for a sound reason: a combination needs at least two variables with missing values, and we have one. I would rather show you the error than draw an empty plot. The takeaway is that `gg_miss_upset()` is a tool for the day your dataset has many `NA`s in several columns, and for that day you now know it exists.

### The clue hiding in a derived column

So far the missing value looks like a small, isolated accident. Before accepting that, I asked a different question, one that no missing-data plot suggests: *what depends on this column?* A value that is blank in the raw file can still leave a fingerprint in every column computed from it. `Pdgfrb_Total` is the natural suspect, since the name says it is the sum of the positive and negative counts.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Do Pos + Neg and Total agree in every row where Neg is present?
with(subset(cell_data, !is.na(Pdgfrb_Neg)),
     all(Pdgfrb_Pos + Pdgfrb_Neg == Pdgfrb_Total))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# And what does the animal with the missing Neg look like?
cell_data |>
  filter(is.na(Pdgfrb_Neg)) |>
  select(MouseID, DPI, Pdgfrb_Pos, Pdgfrb_Neg, Pdgfrb_Total)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  MouseID DPI Pdgfrb_Pos Pdgfrb_Neg Pdgfrb_Total
1    Td79   3        398         NA          398
```


:::
:::






In all 48 animals with a recorded `Pdgfrb_Neg`, `Pdgfrb_Pos + Pdgfrb_Neg` equals `Pdgfrb_Total` exactly. Animal `Td79` is the exception that matters: its `Pdgfrb_Total` is 398, identical to its `Pdgfrb_Pos`, and **not** `NA`. Whoever (or whatever spreadsheet formula) computed the total treated the missing negative count as zero. Think of a plate reader that, faced with an empty well, reports an absorbance of zero instead of "no reading": the column looks complete, and it is quietly wrong.

![An empty well is not a reading of zero. A column that reports 0 for "nothing there" looks complete, and is quietly wrong.](images/eda-missing-data_empty-well-reads-zero.png){#fig-missing-plate fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a microplate on a wooden bench with rows of teal-filled wells and one empty, pale well near the middle. Beside it, a small analog dial rests its needle near the zero mark with a faint green glow, and a pipette lies in front of the plate."}

This is the first real finding of the chapter, and it answers the opening question in a way I did not expect. The `NA` itself is small. The *derived* value built on it is not an `NA` at all, it is a wrong number that looks fine, and it propagates. Any analysis that uses `Pdgfrb_Total`, for instance a proportion `Pdgfrb_Pos / Pdgfrb_Total`, will see this animal as having a PDGFR-β+ share of exactly 100%, which is false (its true share is below 100% by whatever the missing negative count was). I will come back to the consequence for the proportion model in @sec-logistic-regression in the take-home message. For now, notice the habit this suggests: when a column has an `NA`, check every column that was computed from it.

## Three ways a value can go missing

Knowing that a value is missing is half of the problem. The other half is *why*, because the reason decides which analyses are safe. Statisticians sort the reasons into three mechanisms, and I will give you the lab versions first, since you have met all three at the bench.

**The accident.** A rack of tubes is dropped on the floor on a Tuesday afternoon. Which samples are lost has nothing to do with the animal, the day, the treatment or the value you would have measured. Whatever is missing is a random draw from what you had. This is the optimistic case.

**The explained loss.** Sections from the day-3 brains are softer after the ischemic insult and tear more often when you cut them. Now the losses are not random: they are concentrated at day 3. But notice what saves you. *You know which animals were day 3*, because you recorded it. The missingness is explained by something you measured, and within the day-3 animals, which ones tore is no more likely to depend on how many cells they had.

**The informative loss.** The most severe infarcts have a core that crumbles when you cut it, so the sections you could not quantify are *precisely* the ones with the most damage. Or, closer to a familiar problem in survival experiments: the animals that did not make it to day 30 are the ones with the largest lesions, so the day-30 group you analyze is a self-selected survivor group. Here the reason a value is missing is the value itself. This is the nightmare case, because the data you have are a biased sample of the data you wanted, and nothing in the data you have says so.

![A wide-mesh net only keeps the big fish, so every fish you hold looks big. When what's lost depends on the value itself, the data you kept are a biased sample, and nothing in them says so.](images/eda-missing-data_wide-mesh-net.png){#fig-missing-net fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a smiling researcher in a lab coat and green sweater holding a wide-mesh fishing net at the edge of a pond. Three large teal fish are inside the net, while many small ochre fish slip through its holes and leap into the water below."}

Rubin gave these three situations names [@jamshidian2009; @harrell2015]. Let $Y$ be the full set of measurements, which splits into the part you observed, $Y_{\text{obs}}$, and the part that is missing, $Y_{\text{mis}}$. Let $R$ be an indicator that is 1 when a value was observed and 0 when it was lost, and let $\phi$ stand for whatever parameters govern the loss process. The three mechanisms differ in what the probability of being missing is allowed to depend on.

The accident is [missing completely at random]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (MCAR): the chance of loss does not depend on anything in the data.

$$
P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}, \phi) = P(R \mid \phi)
$$ {#eq-mcar}

The explained loss is [missing at random]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (MAR): once you account for what you observed, the chance of loss no longer depends on the values you did not see.

$$
P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}, \phi) = P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, \phi)
$$ {#eq-mar}

The informative loss is [missing not at random]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (MNAR): the chance of loss depends on $Y_{\text{mis}}$ itself, even after accounting for everything you observed.

$$
P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}, \phi) \text{ depends on } Y_{\text{mis}}
$$ {#eq-mnar}

The name "missing at random" is, I think, the worst piece of terminology in this field, because the data are *not* missing at random in the everyday sense; they are missing for reasons that you happen to have recorded. It helps to read @eq-mar as "missing, at random, *given what I measured*".

::: callout-tip
### MAR is a property of your model, not of your column

This is the subtlety that makes the three labels slippery. A column that is MNAR when you ignore the other variables can become MAR once you include the right ones. If the crumbling sections are the ones from big infarcts and you have measured infarct volume, then conditioning on infarct volume can turn an informative loss into an explained one. The label depends on which variables are in the analysis [@harrell2015]. It is also why the work of building a good model for missing data is mostly the work of thinking about *how the data were produced*.
:::

### Can the data tell us which one we have?

I wish the answer were yes. It is partly. You can often detect that missingness is *not* completely random: compare the observed variables between rows with and without a missing value (the day, the condition, the area), and if the groups differ, MCAR is in trouble. Formal versions of this exist, such as Little's MCAR test [@jamshidian2009]. What you cannot do, from the observed data alone, is distinguish MAR from MNAR, because the thing that would settle it, the missing value, is exactly the thing you do not have [@harrell2015; @gelman2020].

With one missing value in 49 rows, even the first comparison is out of reach. We would be comparing a group of 48 animals against a group of one, and a sample of one has no variance to estimate. So here is where the book has to be honest about how little the data can say. All I can offer from the table is a description: `Td79` is a day-3 MCAO animal, whose `Pdgfrb_Pos` count is ordinary, and 1 of the 8 day-3 animals is missing, 0 of 41 at any other day. That is a pattern with a sample size of one, and I would not build a story on it.

What *can* settle the question is knowledge of how the data were produced, which is information from outside the table. If I were analyzing this for a paper I would do three things, in this order. I would ask whoever quantified the sections what happened to `Td79` (a torn section, a failed stain, a blank in the export?), and write the answer next to the cleaning code. I would check whether the same person or batch has other quirks. And, as the next section shows, I would run the analysis a few different ways, including some deliberately pessimistic ones, to see whether anything changes. The `Pdgfrb_Total` clue points toward the first of those explanations being a blank in an export, not a lost slide, since a lost slide would more plausibly have taken `Pdgfrb_Pos` with it. But that is a story that I made up to fit the pattern, in the same spirit as the area-unit story of @sec-eda-data-quality. It is a hypothesis, and the lab notes would say if it is true.

### What the mechanisms do to an estimate

The three definitions are abstract until you watch them bias something, and with one missing value I cannot show you that on `cell_data`. So I will use a small simulation, the kind of generative check @sec-bayesian-core-workflow argued for, where *I* know the truth. I generate 200 measurements $y$ that depend on a recorded variable $z$ (think of $z$ as the day, and $y$ as a cell count), with a true mean of 2. Then I delete about 30% of the $y$ values by each of the three mechanisms: at random, depending on $z$ (the explained loss), and depending on $y$ itself (the informative loss). I estimate the mean of $y$ two ways: from the complete cases only, and from a regression of $y$ on $z$ fitted to the complete cases and then averaged over *all* the $z$ values (this is a stand-in for any method that uses what we recorded about the animals with missing data). I repeat this a thousand times and plot where the estimates land.

I show the spread across simulations as a dot with an interval, and the truth as a vertical line: the question is whether the line lies inside the cloud of estimates. I encode the method with both color and shape.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)

one_sim <- function(n = 200) {
  z <- rnorm(n)
  y <- 2 + 1.5 * z + rnorm(n)
  p_mcar <- rep(0.30, n)
  p_mar  <- plogis(-0.85 + 1.5 * z)
  p_mnar <- plogis(-0.85 + 1.5 * (y - 2) / 1.8)

  est <- function(p, mech) {
    miss <- runif(n) < p
    d <- data.frame(y = y, z = z)[!miss, ]
    c(mech = mech,
      `Complete cases` = mean(d$y),
      `Uses recorded z` = mean(predict(lm(y ~ z, d), newdata = data.frame(z = z))))
  }
  rbind(est(p_mcar, "MCAR"), est(p_mar, "MAR"), est(p_mnar, "MNAR"))
}

sims <- do.call(rbind, replicate(1000, one_sim(), simplify = FALSE)) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-mech, names_to = "method", values_to = "estimate") |>
  mutate(estimate = as.numeric(estimate),
         mech = factor(mech, levels = c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR"))) |>
  group_by(mech, method) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(estimate),
            lo = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
            hi = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(sims, aes(x = mean, y = method, color = method, shape = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), size = 0.8, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~mech, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Complete cases" = "#E69F00",
                                "Uses recorded z" = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Complete cases" = 16, "Uses recorded z" = 17)) +
  labs(x = "Estimated mean of y", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Estimated mean of `y` (truth = 2, vertical line) over 1000 simulated datasets, for three missingness mechanisms and two estimators. Dots are the average estimate; bars cover the middle 95% of estimates across simulations. About 30% of `y` is deleted in each scenario.](eda-missing-data_files/figure-html/fig-missing-mechanisms-1.png){#fig-missing-mechanisms fig-alt='Three stacked panels, one per mechanism: MCAR, MAR, and MNAR. In each, two estimators are shown as a dot with a horizontal bar. In the MCAR panel both estimators sit on the vertical line at 2. In the MAR panel the complete-case estimator sits well to the left of the line while the model-based estimator sits on it. In the MNAR panel both estimators sit to the left of the line.' width=672}
:::
:::






Read it from top to bottom. Under MCAR, both estimators land on the truth: throwing away a random 30% of the animals costs you precision (the bars are wider than they would be with everything) but not accuracy. Under MAR, the complete-case mean is wrong, and by a lot, because the animals with a high $z$ are lost more often and they are also the ones with a high $y$; the estimator that uses the recorded $z$ repairs it. Under MNAR, *both* are wrong, and neither tells you that. This is the figure I would put on a slide titled "why the mechanism matters": the choice of method is only as good as the assumption about how the values were lost, and the assumption cannot be read off the data.

## What to do about it

Now the practical question. Faced with a missing value, you have two broad families of options. You can **drop** the incomplete row and analyze the complete cases, or you can **keep** it and let the analysis account for what is unknown, either by filling in plausible values or by treating the unknown as a quantity to be estimated. I do not think any of these is *the* correct answer, and I would be suspicious of a book that claimed so. Each one is a different bet about the data, and the useful skill is to be able to say which bet you are making. @tbl-missing-options lays them side by side.






::: {#tbl-missing-options .cell tbl-cap='Four ways to handle one missing predictor, and what each one assumes. The right-hand column is the price you pay if the assumption is wrong.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Approach, ~`What it does`, ~`Valid when`, ~`If the assumption fails`,
  "Complete cases (drop the row)",
    "Analyzes only animals with every variable observed.",
    "Missingness is MCAR (or depends only on the predictors, not on the outcome).",
    "Biased estimates, not just lost precision, as in the MAR panel of the figure.",
  "Multiple imputation (`mice`)",
    "Fills each gap with several plausible values drawn from a model, fits the analysis on each completed dataset, and pools the results.",
    "MAR, and the imputation model includes the outcome and the variables that explain the loss.",
    "Biased if the imputation model leaves out a relevant variable, or the loss is MNAR.",
  "Imputation inside the model (`brms` with `mi()`)",
    "Treats each missing value as an unknown parameter, estimated jointly with the regression, with a sub-model for the variable that has gaps.",
    "MAR, and the distribution you assume for the incomplete variable is reasonable.",
    "Biased under MNAR, and sensitive to a poor sub-model (including one that predicts impossible values).",
  "Sensitivity analysis (plug in extremes)",
    "Fills the gap with a low and a high plausible value and checks whether the conclusion moves.",
    "Never 'valid': it is a stress test, useful whatever the mechanism.",
    "Does not apply: it does not claim to estimate the truth, only to bound how much the answer could move."
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(13))
```

The honest summary of that table, and of the textbooks behind it, is that when the fraction of rows with a missing value is tiny, the choice barely matters. Harrell's rule of thumb is that below about 3% of cases with any missing value it makes little difference how you impute, and complete-case analysis is an acceptable option [@harrell2015]. Huntington-Klein makes the same practical point: when the problem is a tiny fraction of the data, the extra complexity of the more sophisticated methods may cost more than it buys [@huntingtonklein2021]. We have 1 row in 49, about 2%. I am going to run all four approaches anyway, not because I expect different answers, but because *seeing* that they agree on a tiny problem is the best way to understand what they would do on a large one.

### A question to ask with the missing predictor

I need a model with an inferential question, and I want to state it in plain language first. `Pdgfrb_Neg` is the count of cells in the region that do **not** express PDGFR-β, a rough measure of how cellular that section is. The question I will ask is: *does knowing the number of PDGFR-β-negative cells tell me anything about the number of PDGFR-β-positive cells, once I know the day?* It is a deliberately modest question, picked because the missing value sits in a *predictor*, and a missing predictor is the case where the choice of method matters, whereas a missing outcome in a standard regression can simply be dropped without bias when the outcome is MAR [@gelman2020]. Treat the model as a vehicle for comparing methods, not as a scientific finding about pericytes.

Two choices to explain. I model the log of `Pdgfrb_Pos`, because the counts are positive and strongly right-skewed; a Gaussian model on the log scale, with a coefficient for each day (`DPI_f`, as in the later chapters), keeps this chapter on the linear model you already know from @sec-intro-applied-modeling. A proper count model is the subject of @sec-count-regression, and nothing about the missing-data logic changes when you swap the likelihood. And I rescale `Pdgfrb_Neg` to hundreds of cells (`neg_100`), so that the coefficient reads as "the change in log count for each 100 more negative cells", on a scale the sampler finds comfortable.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cell_data$DPI_f   <- factor(cell_data$DPI)
cell_data$log_pos <- log(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos)
cell_data$neg_100 <- cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg / 100   # hundreds of cells

complete_rows <- cell_data[!is.na(cell_data$neg_100), ]   # 48 animals
nrow(complete_rows)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 48
```


:::
:::






The four tabs below fit the same regression four ways. Read them with the table above in mind: the first and third drop `Td79`, the second and fourth keep it, and they keep it by different routes. In `brms`, the `mi()` term turns the missing `neg_100` into a parameter, and the second formula, `neg_100 | mi() ~ DPI_f`, is the sub-model that says what we believe about the variable that has the gap: its mean may differ by day, and the day is observed for everyone. That sub-model is where the MAR assumption lives, because it uses what we know (the day) to guess what we do not. `mice` takes the other route, drawing several completed datasets from a similar model (a normal-theory imputation of `neg_100`, using the day *and* the outcome `log_pos`, which is what the textbooks require for an unbiased slope [@harrell2015]) and pooling the 20 resulting fits with Rubin's rules [@mice]. I leave the `brms` priors at their defaults, for the same reason as in the earlier chapters: I want the data to shape the coefficients while we learn the structure.

::: panel-tabset

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(fit_cc)
```

The first thing to check, as always, is that the sampler behaved. For the `mi()` model, the largest Rhat across all parameters is 1.005, the smallest bulk effective sample size is 1150, and the number of divergent transitions is 0. That meets the thresholds from the earlier chapters.

Now the comparison that the whole section was building toward. The coefficient of interest is the one for the number of negative cells, and the question is whether dropping `Td79`, imputing it inside the model, or imputing it with `mice` changes what we would conclude. I add two rows that are not methods at all, but stress tests of the kind the textbooks recommend when the mechanism is in doubt [@jamshidian2009; @harrell2015]: I fill the one gap with the *smallest* and then the *largest* `Pdgfrb_Neg` observed anywhere, refit, and see whether the coefficient moves. The intervals for those two rows are conditional on a guess, so I draw them with a different shape and do not read them as honest uncertainty.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
b_cc <- fixef(fit_cc)["neg_100", ]
b_mi <- fixef(fit_mi)[grep("^logpos_mineg", rownames(fixef(fit_mi))), ]
b_lm <- tidy(lm_cc, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "neg_100")
b_mice <- pooled |> filter(term == "neg_100")

sens <- function(fill) {
  d <- cell_data
  d$neg_100[is.na(d$neg_100)] <- fill
  m <- lm(log_pos ~ DPI_f + neg_100, data = d)
  c(estimate = coef(m)[["neg_100"]], confint(m)["neg_100", ])
}
s_lo <- sens(min(cell_data$neg_100, na.rm = TRUE))
s_hi <- sens(max(cell_data$neg_100, na.rm = TRUE))

compare <- tibble::tribble(

  "Fill with smallest", "Stress test", s_lo[[1]], s_lo[[2]], s_lo[[3]],
  "Fill with largest", "Stress test", s_hi[[1]], s_hi[[2]], s_hi[[3]]

  mutate(approach = factor(approach, levels = rev(approach)))
```

### What `mi()` actually did to `Td79`

I find the `mi()` approach the most instructive of the four, because it makes the imputation visible. The missing count is not hidden inside a preprocessing step: it is a parameter with a posterior, so we can plot it. This is a half-eye, because the *shape* of the posterior is the point here (a wide, lopsided distribution), not just its interval, and I show the seven day-3 animals with an observed `Pdgfrb_Neg` as dots for context.

```{.r .cell-code}
observed_d3 <- cell_data |>
```

Two things stand out, and both are lessons about *assumptions* more than about `Td79`. First, the posterior is wide: the model's best guess is 279 negative cells, with a 95% interval from -96 to 645. That is the honest size of what we know about an animal whose count we never saw, and it is the uncertainty that a single plugged-in value (a mean imputation, say) would have pretended away. Second, and this is the cost of the sub-model: I told the model that `neg_100` is Gaussian, and a Gaussian does not know that a cell count cannot be negative. The share of the posterior below zero is 7.4%, which is impossible for a count. For a tiny problem it is harmless, but it is the kind of assumption that stops being harmless when a larger fraction of the column is missing, and it is why the next step in a serious analysis would be a sub-model that respects the support of the variable (a log-scale or a count sub-model). In `brms`, `mi()` works only with continuous variables, because Stan cannot sample discrete parameters [@mcelreath2020], so a missing count has to be handled through a continuous approximation or be integrated out.

A last sanity check, as the earlier chapters taught: does the `mi()` model reproduce the data it was fit to? A posterior predictive check on the outcome is the same procedure as in @sec-mcmc-model-checking.

### The frequentist equivalent

With one missing value, the Bayesian and frequentist answers are, for practical purposes, the same, and the reason is worth saying plainly. The complete-case `lm` and the complete-case `brms` fit agree because the priors are weak and the likelihood does the work, as in every single-level model so far [@gelman2020]. The `mice` pooled estimate and the `mi()` estimate agree for a deeper reason: both are doing the same thing under the same assumption (MAR), averaging over the plausible values of the one missing count. Multiple imputation does it by drawing 20 completed datasets and combining them with Rubin's rules, and `mi()` does it by sampling the missing value as a parameter at every iteration of the chain. They are two implementations of one idea, and `mi()`'s advantage is that the uncertainty about the missing value flows into the posterior of every other parameter without a separate pooling step.

Where would they diverge? When there is more to lose. With many missing values, the `brms` sub-model and the `mice` imputation model are two different bets about the missing variable, and they can give different answers. With few animals and a weakly identified sub-model, a frequentist imputation model has nothing to regularize it, whereas a prior on the sub-model's parameters can. And in the MNAR case, no choice among these four rescues you: the Bayesian route is to *model the missingness process itself* explicitly, with assumptions you must state and defend, which is what the stress tests above are a crude, honest first step toward.

## Take home message

We started with one `NA` and a question: accident, clue, or problem? My answer, after looking, is "a bit of all three, in different places." As far as the analysis goes, it was an accident: with 1 row in 49, complete cases, imputation inside `brms`, `mice` and even deliberately extreme fills all gave the same answer, which is what the textbooks predict when the missing fraction is below a few percent. As far as the data goes, it was a clue: the `Pdgfrb_Total` of animal `Td79` equals its `Pdgfrb_Pos`, so the total was computed as if the missing negative count were zero, which means the *derived* column is wrong while looking complete. And that is the problem: any analysis that uses `Pdgfrb_Total`, such as the proportion `Pdgfrb_Pos / Pdgfrb_Total` that @sec-logistic-regression models (and from which it leaves this animal out), gives this animal a share of exactly 100%, and that number is an artifact. Checking what is *derived from* a column with an `NA` is the habit I would take from this chapter before any of the packages.

The rest is a way of thinking. MCAR, MAR and MNAR are claims about how the values were lost, they cannot be read off the data (certainly not from one missing value), and they are settled by knowing how the experiment was run. Complete cases, multiple imputation and `mi()` are not rival answers; they are different assumptions, and @tbl-missing-options says which. When the missing fraction is tiny, choose the simplest one you can defend and report that you checked the others. When it is not, the choice starts to matter, and then the lab notes matter more than the package. The next chapter, @sec-eda-ggplot, goes back to the thing EDA is really for, which is to *draw* the data.
